How AI Changes the Four Types of Analytics for Data Scientists

Treat AI agents as junior teammates and move up the abstraction ladder, owning problem framing, model evaluation, and business partnership.

Destin Gong
November 22, 202613 min read
Prefer us on Google

I’ve been thinking about what data science means in the age of AI, and I am definitely not alone in these thoughts. Traditionally, we associate it with machine learning algorithms, predictive modeling, statistics, mathematics, and optimization. I still find these topics fascinating—the elegance of mathematical principles becoming useful algorithms is one of the reasons I enjoy data science in the first place. However, with AI, LLMs, and coding agents emerging, the access to technical knowledge and implementation is increasingly accelerated. This is likely a shared experience that spans most professional fields. As skills that took years to learn become democratized rapidly and easier to apply, what distinguishes an experienced practitioner? In this article, I would like to share my perspective on how data science roles will continue to evolve in the AI era.

Moving Up the Abstraction Ladder

With the rapid growth of AI’s coding capabilities, I notice many responses remain predominantly reactive, such as “Which skills will become obsolete?”, “Will data scientist be replaced by AI?”, or “How do I stay relevant?” Perhaps a better question is how we can proactively leverage AI’s capabilities to our advantage. By reframing our perspective to treat AI agents as collaborators or teammates, our role shifts toward defining what needs to be done and why it matters, rather than focusing on the mechanics of how to do it — this is what I refer to as moving up the abstraction ladder.

The level of abstraction is a concept in computer science and information systems that describes how far we step back from technical details to focus on the broader problem and the decisions it informs. At a lower level, we might write or tune an algorithm; at a higher level, we ask which approach fits the problem, what evidence would make its output useful, and how it should guide action. We have seen a similar shift before where libraries such as scikit-learn let us apply machine learning algorithms without implementing each one from scratch. Now AI takes this further by making natural language the next programming language, abstracting away more details of a subsystem and helping us connect parts of an entire workflow. But greater abstraction does not mean less responsibility. We still need to understand the foundations well enough to guide the work, question assumptions, and evaluate the results.

In some ways, working with an AI agent resembles working with a junior teammate. It can help us explore approaches and produce a first draft quickly, but it may not understand the organization’s priorities, institutional knowledge, data history, or unwritten assumptions unless we provide that guidance.

Data science has conventionally focused on how models work and how to improve performance. Those questions still matter and I am not suggesting we abandon mathematics, statistics, or machine learning. Without these foundations, how could we evaluate AI outputs or recognize when a candidate model is inappropriate in a specific situation? Understanding the underlying principles lets us choose among approaches in different contexts. Technical expertise may become less about manual implementation and more about guiding, challenging, and judging the work done by AI. Perhaps data science will shift from being defined by the models we build to the problems we solve and the impact we generate. I don't have a complete answer yet, but I want to explore whether AI allows us to work at a higher level of thinking—focusing not just on what it replaces, but on what it enables us to achieve.

Redefining Four Fundamental Analytics Capabilities

Moving up the abstraction ladder enables the high-level development of end-to-end ML systems and data products powered by prompts, MCP tools, and AI agents. However, the fundamental concepts behind them remain unchanged, as data science still encompasses four core pillars — descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics. Descriptive analytics tells us what has happened, diagnostic analytics helps us understand why, predictive analytics estimates what might happen next, and prescriptive analytics helps us decide what to do about it. Together, they move us from understanding the past, to extracting fundamental patterns, to making informed decisions about the future and taking actions accordingly.

Descriptive — What has happened?

This is the analytical phase that uncovers patterns in historical data, establishing a picture of existing performance trends and segment profiles (e.g., the top-selling products last quarter, customer age range with the highest churn rate). This stage involves statistical analysis, exploratory data analysis and data visualization techniques. Due to the generalizability and repeatable nature of these techniques, I personally think basic descriptive analytics has already been largely conquered and streamlined by AI tools. As data agents emerge, allowing people with different levels of technical background to chat with data using natural language, we need to consider bringing additional value to describe and interpret what has happened.

Because data science is a multidisciplinary profession, I believe data scientists now hold more responsibility to bridge the gap between statistical results and domain knowledge, translating numbers into quantifiable commercial insights or practical impacts for non-technical audiences. For example, AI might report that sales fell 24% last month. Knowing the business ran a major promotion the month before, I would compare sales with a typical month before drawing the conclusion that the sales drop is a sign of poor performance. This is where a data scientist adds value to descriptive analytics by applying business context to clarify what the numbers mean, rather than treating every decline as a sign that something is going wrong. Data scientists can take this a step further by developing a company-wide, domain-aware semantic orchestration for AI agents to connect quantitative results with business-domain knowledge automatically.

After knowing what has happened already through descriptive analytics, there are two natural pathways: understanding why it happened or predicting what is likely to happen next, which leads to diagnostic or predictive analytics. There are no hard rules of which needs to come first, as they usually complement each other. In some scenarios, inferring future performance using historical data is prioritized to respond promptly before digging into the root cause, hence predictive modeling based on correlation analysis becomes the natural next step. However, predicting something isn't the same as understanding it. The question worth asking is, “Why did it happen?” This is addressed through diagnostic analytics. I would suggest creating an iterative loop in which diagnostic techniques identify key drivers that then feed into predictive modeling for more accurate predictions.

Diagnostic — Why did it happen?

Common diagnostic approaches include driver analysis, which identifies factors associated with an outcome, and contribution analysis, which estimates how different components account for an observed result or change. Additionally, we can use segmentation, cohort comparisons, change-point detection, hypothesis testing, and causal investigation to narrow down and validate potential explanations.

Data scientists cannot catch up with the speed of AI-generated code; instead, we add value by using our judgment to choose techniques suited to the context, assess each method's assumptions and limitations, and determine whether the evidence is strong enough to support a decision. For example, if we want to investigate beyond correlations between data points, we need to guide AI tools towards using causal inference for in-depth investigation. Otherwise, it may identify factors that merely move in the same direction as the dependent variable, rather than the root cause of the changes. A practical example is that ice cream sales and drowning incidents may increase simultaneously. This does not imply that ice cream causes drowning; rather, warmer weather influences both.

Distinguishing causation from correlation is essential in the business context to ensure that investments are directed towards the actual drivers of impact rather than factors that coincide with success. This is one of the most overlooked aspects when we only rely on AI-generated code, because the distinctions can be subtle if merely inspecting the outcome. Data scientists bring important judgment throughout the workflow: frame business problems as appropriate hypothesis testing, design experiments such as A/B tests, collect and evaluate evidence, communicate findings accurately to business users, and reduce the risk of making decisions based on surface-level metrics.

Predictive — What is likely to happen next?

Predictive modeling and machine learning occur at this stage, and they’re what most people associate with data scientists’ day-to-day work. After knowing what’s in the data through descriptive analytics, and explaining likely reasons behind it using diagnostic analytics, predictive analytics then estimate what’s likely to happen next. In the age of AI, we should reframe this stage as empowering stakeholders to stay one step ahead, proactively preparing for emerging trends rather than reacting to changes at the last minute.

Traditionally, data scientists spend most of their time transforming data, building algorithms, and tuning models' hyperparameters to achieve the best evaluation metrics. We used to implement neural networks, random forest, and gradient boosting algorithms by typing down every single line of code. While AI helps with systematically cleaning data, training models and evaluating results, the more valuable data science skill is synthesizing those patterns with business acumen to forecast future outcomes.

A predictive modeling lifecycle typically moves from data discovery to deployment. I will use a demand forecasting case study to illustrate the evolution of data scientists in an AI-assisted workflow.

  • Business understanding and data collection: While AI largely automates writing SQL queries and integration code for data ingestion, data scientists still need to determine which data sources are appropriate for answering business problems. Example: identify the source systems for collecting store-level sales, inventory information, promotion calendars, and public holiday data.

  • Data preprocessing: Shift from manually coding for missing value imputation to guiding data preprocessing decisions. Example: AI tools may automatically fill stores with missing sales data with 0 by default, but we should still investigate why they are missing before choosing data imputation method. Instead of jumping into the conclusion that this is a data quality issue, consider that missing values may highlight edge scenarios or systemic failures in data capture process.

  • Feature engineering: Move away from manually scaling numeric variables and one-hot encoding all categorical variables into numerics values, to selecting meaningful, available signals based on our domain knowledge and avoiding data leakage. Example: To generate a 12-week demand forecast, incorporate a direct competitor’s sales volume as a feature, and validate that AI-generated code excludes any sales recorded after the forecast date to prevent feature leakage.

  • Model training: AI can implement a list of candidate algorithms and tune hyperparameters to achieve the optimal outcome of objective functions, but it remains critical for data scientists to exercise judgment in determining which algorithm’s inductive bias best aligns with the business context. We also need to consider balancing model performance with interpretability. Example: AI may select XGBoost as the best model because it has the lowest prediction error, but it does not fit if business wants an explainable model. Besides, if demand is intermittent, Croston’s method is a better fit to handle sparse demand patterns, whereas XGBoost tends to be sensitive to data drift when datasets are small.

  • Model evaluation: Move beyond reporting statistical metrics and focus more on interpreting them within context to assess their business consequences. For example, we should guide AI to use WAPE over MAPE to assess total demand error across products with different sales volumes, since it weights errors by actual demand, and MAPE can be skewed by very low actuals.

  • Model interpretation: AI can generate code for model explainability and feature importance, but data scientists still need to check that the resulting explanations are faithful to the model and useful for the decision at hand. Example: AI can produce SHAP summaries to indicate features contributing most to model predictions, but a data scientist needs to ensure the interpretation only describes model behavior rather than establish causal effect.

  • Deployment and monitoring: AI can draft deployment code and monitoring reports quickly, while data scientists refine that into a reliable workflow and define thresholds for investigation, retraining, or rollback, and check that predictions remain useful for decisions. Example: AI may detect forecast errors increasing around 15% at several stores, but a data scientist checks whether external factors like holidays explain the change in customer behavior before deciding whether to retrain the model or inform business users.

To move up the abstraction ladder, data scientists should treat predictive modeling as a mechanism to prioritize business decisions and clearly communicate the uncertainty or biases behind these predictions. This ensures business users understand risks at an early stage and can proactively prepare for upcoming changes with confidence.

Prescriptive — What to do about it?

Once we understand what's likely to happen and why, we can make evidence-based recommendations for next best actions. Moving to the stage of prescriptive analytics, we support the business with action plans for stronger impact or stop processes that are not working. Rethinking prescriptive analytics in the age of AI, the value data scientists bring is the ability to translate business objectives into mathematical optimization problems. We work with the business to clarify the requirements, understand the constraints, and identify solutions that are practical to implement. We then communicate those recommendations and explain the operational trade-offs so the business can decide and prioritize potential next steps.

Let's break down prescriptive analytics lifecycle into four stages and look at how they evolve with AI-assisted workflow.

  • Problem formulation: Data scientists start by working with business teams to understand the operating context, agree on primary objectives to improve, and identify key trade-offs and resource limits. AI can assist with translating these into three key components of an optimization problem: objectives, decision variables and constraints.

  • Optimization modeling: AI can quickly implement candidate optimization models and solver code for data scientists to compare. Data scientists select a method based on the types of decisions involved in the real-world scenario, for example linear programming suits decisions that vary continuously, e.g. how many kilograms of grains to stock at a warehouse, while mixed-integer linear programming handles choices.

  • Solution validation: Data scientists play an important role at this stage in verifying that the output reflects the agreed objectives and operating constraints, ensuring that we do not blindly follow AI-generated results that optimize the objective function but fail in real-world scenarios.

  • Rollout and change management: Data scientists work with stakeholders to embed recommendations in day-to-day operations, communicate changes, and monitor adoption and outcomes. This is the part that is difficult for AI to replace, as it involves active communication and empathy while working closely with stakeholders who are driving the changes or those impacted by them.

What Skills Are Crucial in the Age of AI?

1. Judgment and Critical Thinking

Utilize our core technical skills in statistics, machine learning and computer science to evaluate AI-generated code and results. Understand the inductive biases and assumptions behind different algorithms and techniques, then choose the most appropriate approach to align with the business context. For instance, choose Croston’s method when predicting products with intermittent demands, and choose XGBoost when it is critical to capture complex relationships from promotional activities, holidays or store characteristics. Always remain curious and ask why a particular phenomenon occurred, why one model outperforms the other, why the business cares about tackling this problem first. Once the fundamental questions are identified, we leverage our unique expertise to orchestrate AI tools to form the most effective trajectory, implementing a suite of solution pipelines to address these challenges.

2. Business Partnership

Harness empathy and active communication to bridge technical jargon and practical implications, drawing on analogies and concrete use cases. For example, explain how predictive accuracy can increase confidence in estimated economic returns. Additionally, providing explainable solutions and observability on top of black box models are critical to bringing business stakeholders along with the journey for ongoing collaborations.

We will be acting as a trusted partner to empower business professionals to uncover hidden data patterns (descriptive), explain the fundamental root causes (diagnostic), anticipate the likely outcomes (predictive), and enable them to act proactively (prescriptive). Just like a doctor, start by understanding what are the symptoms, diagnosing the underlying reasons, projecting how the disease may develop over time and then prescribing the patient with the best treatment plan.

3. High-Level Thinking

As AI becomes increasingly capable of operational execution, we must move up the abstraction ladder to gain a holistic view of end-to-end solution design. Instead of focusing narrowly on technical aspects, such as which algorithm to choose or which metric to use for model evaluation, we need to deliver cohesive products that empower stakeholders with self-serve commercial insights. This accelerates the transition from data to decisions, and to actions. To achieve this, we must constantly broaden our knowledge across various domains and develop strategic thinking to design sustainable, scalable data products.

···

Key Takeaways

AI gives us an opportunity to rethink the role of data science. Here are some key aspects that can turn our capability into impact:

  • Move up the abstraction ladder: Treat AI as a collaborator while taking responsibility for the problem, approach, and outcome.

  • Connect the four analytics capabilities: Rethink descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics to bridge the gap between technical solutions and business understanding through AI-assisted workflow.

  • Apply judgment, critical thinking, and strategic business partnership: Use technical foundations to question assumptions, evaluate AI-generated work, and choose approaches that fit the business context, while bringing empathy and clear communication to decisions and building sustainable data products that turn insights into action.
